name: Dysraphism with Stalk

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Radiological Criteria for Dysraphism with Stalk

criteria.description: Identification of a fibrous stalk connecting the spinal cord to the dorsal skin or subcutaneous tissue on MRI
Evidence of tethered spinal cord with limited cord mobility on imaging or intraoperative findings
Presence of midline cutaneous markers such as a dermal sinus or small skin dimple overlying the lesion

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of fibrous stalk on imaging plus evidence of spinal cord tethering
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily based on MRI findings supported by clinical features.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Fibrous stalk tethering spinal cord to dorsal skin
pathognomonic.notes: Visualized on MRI as a fibrous band connecting spinal cord to skin
searchTerms: fibrous band tethering spinal cord to skin
spinal cord stuck to back skin

pathognomonic.symptomName: Cutaneous midline dimple or dermal sinus tract
pathognomonic.notes: Often present at the site of the stalk
searchTerms: skin dimple or sinus tract on midline back
small pit or tract in skin along spine

common.notes: Due to tethered cord affecting spinal cord function
Neurogenic bladder due to spinal cord involvement

common.symptomName: Back pain localized to lesion site

searchTerms: sensory loss in feet and legs

occasional.notes: Excess hair growth at the site of spinal dysraphism
Such as clubfoot or pes cavus

rare.notes: Cystic dilation of central canal associated with tethering
Due to chronic spinal cord traction
searchTerms: tightness and muscle spasms in legs

rare.notes: Rare vascular skin anomaly associated with dysraphism
searchTerms: vascular skin tumor on affected area

imaging: MRI demonstrating fibrous stalk connecting spinal cord to dorsal skin
MRI evidence of tethered spinal cord with low-lying conus medullaris
Possible associated syringomyelia on spinal imaging
other: Intraoperative confirmation of fibrous stalk and tethered cord
Presence of cutaneous markers such as dermal sinus or dimple

distinguishingFeatures: Absence of fibrous stalk connecting spinal cord to skin
May have fatty filum terminale or lipoma instead
Presence of lipomatous mass rather than fibrous stalk
Different MRI characteristics with fatty tissue

redFlags: Progressive lower limb weakness or paralysis
Loss of bladder or bowel control
Rapidly worsening back pain or neurological deficits
references: Talamonti G, et al. Spinal dysraphism with stalk: clinical and radiological features. Neurosurg Rev. 2018.
Kothbauer KF. Tethered cord syndrome in children. Neurosurg Focus. 2007.
